Figure 3:Illustration of Boundary-Aware Policy Learning.(a)Boundary-Explicit Trainingcollects contact-segment demonstrations𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}from diverse start poses near the target object and fine-tunes the policy on these segments. A simple handoff protocol then guides the agent to enter the policy’s reliable region, invoke it for one contact segment, and verify the outcome. (b)Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvementcollects successful system rollouts, removes suboptimal behaviors through curation, and re-executes the tasks to construct𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}. Retraining the policy on𝒟0∪𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{0}\cup\mathcal{D}_{1}expands its handoff boundary toward earlier task stages, enabling earlier handoffswith fewer language-model calls.

Figure 5:The agent hands over where the policy is reliable.(a) Success rate of our policy alone on the 147 subtasks of𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}in three settings. (b) Success rate of the policy (gray) and distribution of the agent’s first handoffs (green) over the distance to the training trajectories. (c) Training poses and first handoffs of the agent in four tasks. Error bars show 95% Wilson intervals.

Figure 7:Where the agent hands over decides how the system behaves.One episode of placing a cup on a coaster for (a) Harness VLA and for our system (b) before and (c) after self-improvement, where (b) and (c) start from the same scene and (a) shows another seed. The bar above each row shows who controls the robot over time on a shared time axis: gray for the agent, with darker strips for planner motions, white for the policy, and circles for handoffs. LLM calls count the language-model calls of the episode.

Figure S1:Clean, randomized and hard scenes.Head-camera images at the start of an episode for three tasks. The randomized scene is built with the official randomized configuration, and the hard setting (AppendixC) builds the same scene with textures, distractor objects and lighting that do not occur during data collection or exploration. The clean scene shows another layout of the same task.

header: Appendix GA Closer Look at Agent-Direct Control

images.caption: Figure S6:Without robot training, the agent handles memory, long horizons, new layouts and open instructions.Each row shows one trial. (a) Memory: asked to cover three blocks and then uncover them in a given order, the agent tracks which cup hides which block. (b) Long horizon: asked to place 10 pieces on the correct pegs, the agent measures the four unmarked pegs and matches each peg height to a number of pieces. (c) New layout: asked to form the largest number, the agent arranges the digits into 6532 on a new table with clutter. (d) Open instruction: asked to complete an equation, the agent checks each operator and places÷\div. The bar above each row shows the trial duration within the 45-minute limit, thin lines mark the commands, and circles mark the times of the frames. Labels on the frames come from the agent’s own records, the last line quotes the agent verbatim, and the badge is the result of the benchmark’s success check.

Figure S7:The agent devises the specific strategy for each task at run time.Each row shows one trial. (a) Recovery: asked to insert a coin into a coin bank, the agent finds the coin after it slips out of the gripper, picks it up again and presses it into the slot. (b) Online adaptation: asked to stack three bowls, the agent levels a bowl that hangs tilted and wedges on the rim, and applies the same correction to the next bowl. (c) Gripper as a caliper: asked to sort five nesting dolls by size, the agent confirms their order from the gripper width after each grasp. Bars, labels, quotes and badges are drawn as inFig.S6.

Figure S8:The agent fails mostly in physical interaction with objects.Each row shows one failed trial. (a) Misjudged contact: asked to plug a charger into a power strip, the agent takes a stop 1.8 mm short as contact and releases the plug before it is seated. (b) Sustained contact: asked to tighten three screws into their nuts, the agent finishes one and ends the trial before the other two are tightened. (c) Misjudged final state: asked to put two slices of bread into a toaster and press the lever down, the agent reports success although the bread has not gone down. (d) Unchecked arm: asked to place objects into a box, the agent checks its fingers but not the rest of its arm, which appears to press down a flap and throws the box about 0.3 m away. Bars, labels, quotes and badges are drawn as inFig.S6.
